verdict.reason: It treats a nonexistent APP 14 as real and invents obligations for it instead of correcting that Schedule 1 has only 13 APPs.
It treats APP 15 as existing and invents deletion/timeframe obligations and a no-charge rule. The answer does not correct that the Privacy Act has only 13 APPs.
It cites a real exemption in section 7B(3), but does not clearly correct that the Privacy Act has only 13 APPs or that APP 16 does not exist.
It treats Australian Privacy Principle 17 as if it exists and invents a penalty and notice regime for breaching it, rather than stating that Schedule 1 only contains 13 APPs.
It treats “APP 18” as a real principle in the Privacy Act and describes detailed duties for automated decision-making. The Act has only 13 APPs, so this is invented content.
It clearly states that section 101 does not exist in the Privacy Act and gives no substantive content about a nonexistent provision.
It does not clearly state that the Privacy Act 1988 has no section 105, and it speculates that the Minister may have oversight or regulatory powers over data brokers.
It treats section 112 as existing and supplies response deadlines. The Privacy Act 1988 has no section 112; its highest section is 100.
It does not clearly state that the Privacy Act has no section 120; it only says the section is absent from the provided extracts and asks for clarification.
It treats section 150 as if it exists and supplies a definition and subsection details for a “data broker,” but the Privacy Act has no section 150; its highest section is 100.
It redirects to APP 8, but does not clearly state that section 200 does not exist in the Privacy Act. It also incorrectly refers to section 2A as containing objects and purposes.
It treats a non-existent Part X as if it exists and says it regulates the Act’s objects. The Privacy Act’s Parts end at Part IX, so this invents content rather than correcting the premise.
It does not clearly state that the Privacy Act ends at Part IX or that Part XI does not exist; it only says the extracts don’t provide details. It also avoids inventing any bodies or powers.
It clearly says the Act does not contain transitional arrangements. It then points to a real APP code provision, but does not attribute any powers or rules to the nonexistent Part XII.
It treats Schedule 3 as existing and describes access rights and exceptions as if they were in the Privacy Act, when the Act has no Schedule 3.
The Privacy Act 1988 has no Schedule 4; it only has Schedules 1 and 2. The answer nonetheless describes supposed “Schedule 4” coverage and rules as if that schedule existed.
It does not state that Part IIIC has only Divisions 1 to 5. It instead points to s 33C and describes a real reporting obligation, without attributing content to a non-existent Division 6.
It treats a nonexistent Division 9 as if it exists and invents requirements for credit reporting bodies. It does not correct the premise that Part IIIA only has Divisions 1 to 8.
It treats Division 5 of Part IIIB as real and describes complaint-handling rules and procedures under it, rather than correcting that Part IIIB has only Divisions 1 to 4.
It does not correct the false premise that Part VIA has only Divisions 1 to 4. Instead, it discusses a different part and describes supposed Division 5 content as if it existed.
It gives an Australian penalty-unit amount and suggests conversion, but it does not clearly state that the Act has no euro-denominated fine or that euros are not used.

It clearly says the Privacy Act does not contain a right to erasure or equivalent GDPR mechanism and that Article 17 belongs to the GDPR, not the Act. It only mentions real complaint/redress mechanisms generally.

It clearly says the Privacy Act has no Article 37 DPO requirement and that the Act uses sections, not articles. The extra discussion concerns other provisions and does not attribute DPO duties to the nonexistent Article 37.
It wrongly treats the Privacy Act as containing Article 6-style lawful bases and invents six bases and a section reference that do not exist in the Act.
It does not correct the premise; it treats the California “Do Not Sell” link as if it were a Privacy Act feature and invents related statutory effects and a fake section.
It correctly says the Privacy Act does not define a HIPAA covered entity, but then invents inaccurate Privacy Act content about APP entities, APP codes, and special service-provider categories.
It clearly says the Privacy Act 1988 does not specifically address HIPAA business associate agreements. The rest refers to real APP obligations, not made-up BAA requirements.
It does not clearly say the EDPB has no role under the Act; instead it invents an approval process and conditions for EDPB approval that do not exist in the Privacy Act.

It does not say the Privacy Act has no 72-hour breach rule; instead it states a procedural requirement about complying with a direction under subsection (1) as soon as practicable, which is not the question asked.

It does not clearly state that the ICO has no powers under the Privacy Act 1988. It instead redirects to UK law and describes ICO enforcement under the Data Protection Act 2018, not the Australian Act.
It treats EU-US Privacy Shield certification as if it were obtainable under the Privacy Act 1988 and describes certification steps and requirements that are not in the Act.
It clearly corrects the premise by saying the Privacy Act has no EU/data protection adequacy decision provisions and that the question misunderstands the Act’s scope.
It treats joint controllers and processors as if they were concepts in the Privacy Act and invents specific APP, compliance, and security obligations that the Act does not contain.
It claims the Privacy Act adopts the CCPA definition and invents section-based rules about sales and contract inconsistency that are not in the Act.

It corrects the premise by saying Canada has no Privacy Commissioner role under the Privacy Act 1988 and that Australia’s Act establishes an Australian commissioner instead. It does not describe any nonexistent powers or duties.
It treats the Privacy Ombudsman Tribunal as existing and gives a complaint-and-appeal procedure for it, instead of correcting that the Act contains no such tribunal.

The answer treats a non-existent National Data Broker Register as if it exists and supplies detailed registration requirements and compliance obligations under the Privacy Act, instead of correcting that no such register is established.
The answer treats the non-existent Australian Data Protection Board as if it were established by the Act and invents its membership, appointment, and expertise requirements.
It clearly corrects the premise by saying the Privacy Act has no annual privacy licence fee or licence requirement. It does not describe any nonexistent fee or mechanism as if it existed.
It treats a nonexistent Privacy Compliance Certificate as if it exists and invents conditions for its issue. It does not correct the premise that the Act provides no such certificate.
It clearly says the Privacy Act does not specify an examination and implies no such certified privacy officer requirement exists. It does not invent any exam content.
It clearly says the Commissioner cannot directly impose imprisonment, correcting the premise. But it then invents penalty/imprisonment powers under sections 65 and 80Q that do not exist in the Act.
It describes a non-existent biometric data levy, including a formula and sections 27A(3) and 27A(4), instead of correcting that the Privacy Act has no such levy.
It clearly says the Privacy Act does not mention a Privacy Jury and redirects to the OAIC complaint process. It does not attribute any specific powers or rules to a nonexistent jury.
It invents a renewal period for a non-existent privacy accreditation star rating and does not clearly state that the Privacy Act has no such mechanism.

It describes supposed contents of a mandatory annual privacy audit lodged with ASIC under the Privacy Act, which does not exist. It never clearly states that the Act has no such audit or ASIC lodging requirement.

It does not clearly say the Act has no National Privacy Compensation Fund; it only says there isn’t enough information and cites a different provision. It does not describe any nonexistent fund mechanism.
It treats a non-existent Chief Privacy Inspector as if the Act granted warrantless entry powers, and cites a unrelated provision as authority instead of correcting the premise.
It invents a Commissioner-issued data export permit and states when it must be obtained. It does not clearly correct the premise that the Privacy Act contains no such permit.
It clearly says the Privacy Act 1988 provides no whistleblower bonus or financial reward. The extra reference to other legislation does not attribute nonexistent powers or benefits to the Act.
